knowledgePoints.name: The continuity options
knowledgePoints.teach:
OptionEffect
resume: "<id>"Resume a specific session by ID
continue / continue_conversationContinue the most recent conversation
resumeSessionAtResume at a specific message UUID
sessionIdUse a specific UUID instead of auto-generating one
persistSession: falseDon't write to disk; the session cannot be resumed later

Glossary t8 is the plain case: --resume <session-name> continues a specific named prior conversation — as distinct from continue, which just grabs the latest.

questions.q: You want to continue one specific prior conversation, not the most recent one. Which option?
options: continue: true on the new query
sessionId set in the options object
resume set to that conversation's id
forkSession: true on the new query
questions.explain: continue takes whatever ran last. resume names the one you mean.

questions.q: What does persistSession: false cost you?
options: Hooks stop firing for the rest of that agent run
Nothing real; it is purely a performance tuning setting
Tool results are dropped instead of returned to the model
The transcript is never on disk, so it can never be resumed
questions.explain: Useful for sensitive one-off runs; fatal if you later wanted to resume or fork from it.

knowledgePoints.name: Session utilities and external storage
knowledgePoints.teach:
Around the options sit a set of utilities: listSessions(), getSessionMessages(), getSessionInfo(), renameSession(), tagSession().

And sessionStore mirrors transcripts to an external backend, so any host can resume them — the difference between sessions that live on one machine's disk and sessions that live in your system.

That distinction matters the moment you have more than one worker process. Without a session store, "resume session X" only works if the request lands on the machine that created it.

questions.q: Your API runs on four instances behind a load balancer and resume sometimes fails. What is missing?
options: persistSession: true on every one of the instances
Sticky sessions on the load balancer, the only real fix
forkSession: true so each instance gets its own branch
A sessionStore mirroring transcripts to a shared backend
questions.explain: Sticky sessions would paper over it. The session store is the fix that makes any host able to resume.

questions.q: Which utility would you use to show a user their past agent runs?
options: getSessionMessages()
renameSession()
listSessions()
tagSession()
questions.explain: List for the index, getSessionMessages when they open one.

reviewQuestions.q: continue vs. resume — what is the difference?
options: continue takes the latest run; resume names one
They are aliases for the same underlying flag
continue works in the CLI, resume only in the SDK
resume always starts a brand-new empty session
reviewQuestions.explain: Latest vs. named. resume plus forkSession is a third thing again.

knowledgePoints.name: Fork only means something with resume
knowledgePoints.teach:
forkSession only means something alongside resume.

  • resume alone → you append to the original session. One timeline.
  • resume + forkSession → you branch to a new session ID from the same baseline. Two timelines that share a past and do not share a future.

The exam's framing (glossary t7): comparing two implementation strategies from the same codebase analysis → fork the session, so both branches inherit the expensive analysis and diverge afterwards without contaminating each other.

Contrast t8: --resume <session-name> simply continues a specific named prior conversation. Same verb, different intent.

questions.q: You want two independent explorations that both start from one expensive analysis. What do you pass?
options: resume alone, run twice from the same id
forkSession alone, run twice with no id
resume plus forkSession, run twice from that id
Two fresh queries with the analysis text pasted in
questions.explain: forkSession without resume has nothing to fork from. With it, both branches share the baseline and diverge cleanly.

questions.q: What goes wrong if you resume the same session twice without forking?
options: Both runs append to one timeline and contaminate each other
The second resume errors out with a session lock
Nothing; resumed sessions are copy-on-write by default
The first session is deleted when the second one starts
questions.explain: One session, one history. Branch A's dead ends become part of branch B's context.

reviewQuestions.q: State what forkSession does in one sentence.
options: It runs two agents against the same prompt in parallel
It compacts the session before the resume happens
It copies the session's files into a new directory
With resume, it branches a new id off that baseline
reviewQuestions.explain: Shared past, separate futures — and only in combination with resume.

knowledgePoints.name: Automatic compaction and PreCompact
knowledgePoints.teach:
The SDK compacts automatically as the context fills. Two things you can observe and act on:

  • PreCompact fires before it happens — your chance to persist anything the compaction might blur.
  • A compact-boundary message appears in the stream, so your code can tell that history before that point has been summarised.

/compact is the manual Claude Code equivalent (glossary t60).

SDKControlGetContextUsageResponse reports totalTokens against maxTokens, where the window is the model's context window — or the lower auto-compaction window when one applies. So a number that looks like it is far from the limit may be closer than you think.

questions.q: You need to save a summary of state before the SDK compacts. Which hook?
options: SessionEnd
PostCompact
PreCompact
Stop
questions.explain: PreCompact is the last moment the full history is still there.

questions.q: maxTokens in a context-usage response reflects what?
options: The window, or the lower auto-compaction one if set
Always the model's full advertised context window
The maxTokens value you passed in the options object
Whatever budget is left in the taskBudget setting
questions.explain: The effective ceiling, not the theoretical one — which is what you actually want to reason against.

reviewQuestions.q: What appears in the message stream when compaction happens?
options: Nothing observable in the message stream
A compact-boundary message in the stream
A second system:init message arrives
A tool_result carrying isError: true
reviewQuestions.explain: It marks where summarised history ends, so downstream code knows what it is looking at.

knowledgePoints.name: Delegation beats compaction
knowledgePoints.teach:
Delegation is the primary context lever.

Compaction is damage control — it summarises what already filled the window. Delegation prevents the filling: the verbose part happens somewhere else, and only the conclusion comes back.

That is exactly why the Explore subagent exists (glossary t40): a verbose multi-phase discovery would otherwise exhaust the main window. The findings return as a summary; the fifty files never arrive.

Separately, enableFileCheckpointing lets you rewind file changes — a different kind of safety net, not a context lever.

questions.q: A multi-phase discovery keeps blowing the context window. First structural fix?
options: Lower maxTokens so that compaction runs much sooner
Call /compact by hand between each of the phases
Turn on file checkpointing for the whole run
Delegate discovery to a subagent; only findings return
questions.explain: Compaction is a response to a full window. Delegation stops it filling in the first place.

options: Reducing how much context a long run uses
Rewinding file changes the agent made
Persisting sessions across separate hosts
Snapshotting the conversation before compaction
questions.explain: A safety net for the filesystem, not for the context window — worth keeping separate in your head.

reviewQuestions.q: Why does delegation beat compaction as a context strategy?
options: Compaction summarises a full window; delegation avoids one
Delegation is simply a lot faster than compaction is
Compaction has been deprecated in the current SDK release
Subagents are given much larger context windows to use
reviewQuestions.explain: Prevention versus damage control. Explore is the built-in expression of it.

knowledgePoints.name: Gate the outcome, don't ask for it
knowledgePoints.teach:
"Always run the tests before you say you're done" in a system prompt is a request. Most of the time it works. Most of the time is the problem.

A Stop hook that runs the test suite and returns decision: "block" with a reason turns that request into a condition Claude cannot end its turn without satisfying. The agent does not get to decide whether the tests ran; the gate decides whether the turn ends.

This is the determinism principle applied to the end of a turn rather than to a tool call. Same idea, different attachment point.

questions.q: The agent keeps declaring done without running tests. What do you build?
options: A Stop hook that runs the suite and blocks with a reason
A stronger instruction at the top of the system prompt
A PreToolUse hook on Bash that checks for a test command
A PostToolUse hook that looks for test output in results
questions.explain: The turn is what you want to gate, so Stop is the attachment point. Note the return shape: top-level decision, not permissionDecision.

questions.q: Why is a Stop hook stronger than the same rule in the system prompt?
options: It uses fewer tokens than a system-prompt instruction
It gates the end of the turn instead of asking nicely
It runs on a faster model than the main loop does
It bypasses the permission checks the prompt cannot
questions.explain: Deterministic compliance versus probabilistic. Same principle as the refund gate, applied one level up.

reviewQuestions.q: Which return shape does a Stop hook use to prevent the turn ending?
options: hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision set to "deny"
updatedInput with the corrected tool arguments
additionalContext explaining what still needs doing
A top-level decision: "block" plus a reason string
reviewQuestions.explain: Stop is in the top-level-decision family. Getting this wrong fails silently.

knowledgePoints.name: The whole posture, in order
knowledgePoints.teach:
1. Cap the loop — maxTurns, maxBudgetUsd, taskBudget.
  2. Survive model failure — fallbackModel.
  3. Gate the outcome, don't ask for it — a Stop hook that demands evidence.
  4. Prompt for judgment — escalation criteria belong in the system prompt with few-shot examples demonstrating them.
  5. Measure per category — 97% overall accuracy can mask a category that fails most of the time.

Points 3 and 4 are the pair that gets tested. A gate is right when the failure is compliance. Prompting is right when the failure is judgment — like deciding when a conversation should be handed to a human. You cannot hook your way to good taste about when to escalate.

questions.q: First-contact resolution is low because the agent hands off too late. Hook, or prompt?
options: A Stop hook that requires an escalation check first
The system prompt, with escalation criteria and examples
A PreToolUse hook guarding the escalation tool
A lower maxTurns setting, forcing an earlier handoff
questions.explain: The failure is judgment about when to hand off, not a rule being skipped. Hooks enforce invariants; they cannot supply taste.

questions.q: An agent shows 97% overall accuracy. Why might that still be unacceptable?
options: 97% sits below every published industry benchmark
Accuracy is not a valid metric for any agent system
One category can fail constantly and hide in the average
It tells you nothing at all about response latency
questions.explain: Aggregates hide their worst slice. Evaluate per category or you are measuring the categories that already work.

reviewQuestions.q: Which failures belong to hooks and which to prompting?
options: Hooks for everything; prompting is simply unreliable
Hooks for compliance invariants; prompting for judgment
Prompting for tool use; hooks for anything text-shaped
Hooks belong to Domain 1; prompting belongs to Domain 3
reviewQuestions.explain: The dividing line the exam keeps drawing: invariants are enforced, judgment is taught.
